newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Guns and ruins taint Chechnya's "freedom".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Guns and ruins taint Chechnya's "freedom".

text.p: Chechnya's war with Russia ended six months ago, but shots still ring out regularly from the central market in the ruined capital Grozny.

Alongside the makeshift restaurants selling freshly-grilled meat from tents and the open air billiard tables, in the shadow of a burned-out shell of a building, groups of men buy and sell arms, testing them by firing in the air.

Two dollar-hand grenades, leather holsters, boxes of bullets and optic sights are laid out on tables like the vegetables on sale nearby. The Kalashnikov assault rifles, pistols and daggers carried by the loitering crowd are also on offer.
"I took it from a Russian officer," said Salan Litayev, fingering an American-made Browning pistol.
"You can buy anything here, an anti-aircraft gun, even a tank," he said with a mischievous grin, raising a laugh from the other traders, bundled up in overcoats and fur hats.
WEAPONS A WAY OF LIFE IN SHATTERED CHECHNYA

Chechens grabbed piles of weapons from the battlefield after humiliating Russian troops in 21 months of fighting over the region's independence. They boast that they bought many more from disillusioned and often hungry Russian soldiers.
"Russia doesn't give us any money so we take their weapons and are feeding ourselves," said Vakha Dzhabrailov, adding that supplies were still coming from the cash-strapped Russian army.

President Boris Yeltsin, who agreed to withdraw the troops from Chechnya under a peace deal last August, has accepted the January 27 election of Aslan Maskhadov as the region's president and sent a representative to his inauguration last week.
Yeltsin has also made a public pledge to help rebuild the homes, schools and hospitals destroyed in the campaign against Maskhadov's rebels which killed tens of thousands of people.
But there is a catch.

The 1997 budget, awaiting Yeltsin's signature after being passed by both houses of parliament, sets aside some 750 billion roubles ($130 million) for Chechnya, but only if the separatists back down and accept Russian hegemony.

Without those funds the prospects look bleak. Most of the factories, shops and farms of the rural, mountanous, landlocked region were destroyed in the fighting and the sharp businessmen who got rich in the chaotic early years of Russian reforms have moved to Moscow. Back home, weapons have become a way of life.
TRADITIONS NO LONGER KEEP CRIME IN CHECK
Grozny is full of armed men. On their own or in groups, they hang around in the ruined city centre, some part of new security structures, others with dubious intentions.

Dzhabrailov defended his business by saying that carrying arms was traditional for the Moslem people of the North Caucasus. "Our grandfathers carried weapons before the Soviets came, but they forbade it," he said.

This is one reason why the new government will find it difficult, if not impossible to check the spread of weapons. But Mayerbek Amemsultanov, chief doctor at Chechnya's main remaining hospital, says there is a big difference between then and now.
The traditional strict code of blood-for-blood vengeance among Chechens which used to keep crime at bay no longer applied, he said, giving way to a typical post-war crime wave.
"Virtually every day someone comes in who has been injured in an everyday situation," he said. "In one case it might be theft, in another a fight, in a third an attack."

Appeals for information on the whereabouts of missing people appear regularly on Chechnya's local television channel. "Some of them were killed in the war, but others have disappeared since," said 22-year-old Lyalya Akhayev, who, like many Grozny residents, lives in fear for her life.
Across the road, a Russian woman living alone has recently disappeared. Lyalya suspects that she may be the latest victim of a spiral of murders, kidnappings and armed robberies.
"The house is empty now, but if someone moves in, then we'll know," she said. "They target the Chechens for their money and the Russians for their homes."
The brutality of months of war have inured both attackers and victims to violence and death.
People relentlessly discuss horrors they have witnessed; Russian troops throwing grenades into basements where families are sheltering or rebels burning soldiers alive in their tanks.

For those who have not seen enough, videos on sale in the market include scenes so gruesome they would be banned in many countries: a Russian prisoner of war having his throat slit by a separatist fighter; headless corpses strewn about a street.
Revisiting such atrocities is the only form of therapy in a place where there is no psychiatric help. Patients from before the conflict have been turned out of their ruined hospitals.
"They are all dispersed," said Amemsultanov. "Some have been collected by relatives, others wander around with weapons."
ONLY JOBS WILL STOP THE CRIME WAVE

But he does not believe they are the main reason for the crime which threatens to engulf Chechnya -- a far greater danger in this politically-homogenous region than the civil war gleefully predicted by hardline Russian politicians.

"There are very many young people who are armed to the teeth, they are young, energetic and there is nowhere for them to get a crust of bread through honest means. So they steal, rob, murder," said Amemsultanov.
"Until we create workplaces for the population, it will be hard to deal with this."
With Russia playing a last card in the effort to stop Chechnya splitting away and the international community afraid to step in, this seems an unlikely prospect.

Most of the staff have not been paid since June at Amemsultanov's Hospital Number Nine, Chechnya's only full-time emergency hospital. It has no heating or running water and patients have to buy their own medicines and provide bandages.
The international aid organisations which provided a lifeline pulled out their key staff in December after six Red Cross workers were shot dead in their beds by unknown gunmen.
The quietly-spoken Maskhadov, a white-haired, 46-year-old former Soviet colonel, is painfully aware of his predicament.

"We have to free the nation from violence and the mockery of criminal elements," he said at his inauguration, which began with a rendering of the moving and defiant Chechen anthem and ended with the firing of hundreds of Kalashnikovs in the air.
"A state cannot consider itself free whose citizens are in constant fear for their lives."
